query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled, thin alumina-forming surface treatment (via chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation to deposit an Al-rich precursor layer) will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys by promoting the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent α-Al2O3 scale.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys in their as-cast state, comprising refractory elements such as Mo, Nb, Ta, and W with heterogeneous microstructures.
generation.intervention: A controlled thin alumina-forming surface modification deposited on the alloy via processes such as chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation of an Al-rich precursor.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidizing environment (air, ~21% O2) at 1100–1200°C for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, well-adherent α-Al2O3 scale formed from the Al-rich surface layer.
generation.mechanism: The deposited Al-rich layer oxidizes preferentially to form stable α-Al2O3, which acts as an effective barrier to oxygen ingress, thereby reducing the rate of oxidation and scale spallation compared to the heterogeneous and less protective oxide scales formed on untreated alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show significantly reduced weight gain and improved oxidation resistance (i.e., more uniform and adherent oxide scale) relative to the untreated sample under the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEAs that develop mixed oxide scales (e.g., CrTaO4-based with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3) showing higher weight gain and potential for scale spallation over prolonged exposure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected specifically under prolonged high-temperature oxidation (1100–1200°C for 100 hours) in air; deviations in temperature, exposure time, or non-uniform coating quality may limit or negate the protection.
generation.uncertainty: While alumina is known for its superior oxygen barrier properties, the exact magnitude of improvement in weight gain reduction and scale durability is uncertain and may depend on the coating uniformity and process parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with the alumina-forming surface treatment (via CVD or pack cementation) and a control set left untreated. Expose both sets to air at 1100–1200°C for 100 hours under identical conditions. After exposure, assess the samples by measuring weight gain per unit area, examining the oxide scale morphology via SEM/EDS, and evaluating the adherence of the oxide scale using standard adhesion tests.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scale (e.g., scratch test or bend test)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and an improvement in oxide scale uniformity and adherence relative to the untreated control, the hypothesis that the alumina-forming treatment improves high-temperature oxygen resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. decision.trend: Early work on refractory HEAs for high‐temperature oxidation resistance first focused on allowing the alloys to form in‐situ protective oxide scales – for instance, the formation of a protective CrTaO4‐based oxide layer showed that a continuous, adherent scale can dramatically slow oxidation at 1100 °C (PMC6513993). More recent work has shifted toward engineered surface modifications, as exemplified by the use of oxidation‐resistant coatings (e.g., hafnium coatings that develop a diffusion-bonded transition layer with the substrate in PMC10488483) to preempt the detrimental oxidation of untreated surfaces. These approaches have improved performance compared to untreated alloys but still face challenges such as non-uniform scale growth, inadequate adhesion, and insufficient durability under prolonged exposure.
decision.unsolved: The outstanding problem remains how to reliably and simply modify the as‐cast, untreated alloy surface to encourage the formation of a continuous, stable, and adherent protective oxide at extreme temperatures (around 1100–1200 °C) under oxidizing conditions over long durations (e.g., 100-hour exposures). Existing methods either depend on the uncertain kinetics of in‐situ scale formation or involve complex coatings that may fail under service conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled, thin alumina-forming surface treatment—such as a chemical vapor deposition or pack cementation process to deposit an Al-rich precursor layer—which, upon exposure at 1100–1200 °C in air (~21% O2) for 100 hours, transforms into a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing α-Al2O3 scale.
decision.why: This next step follows naturally from the trend: after demonstrating that in-situ oxide formation (e.g. CrTaO4-based) and conventional coatings have limitations, engineering the alloy surface to induce a well-known, durable alumina scale leverages decades of high-temperature oxidation research in other alloys. Alumina's superior oxygen barrier properties and its established protective mechanisms make it a plausible lever to improve oxidation resistance, directly addressing the gap identified in untreated refractory HEAs.
